html:
In 2015 more than a million people crossed into Europe to ask for asylum, the most in a single year since the Second World War. The largest group came from Syria, fleeing the civil war, with many also from Afghanistan and Iraq.

Most had first fled to Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, part of the wider Syrian refugee crisis. As aid ran short and the war dragged on, many paid smugglers to cross the short stretch of sea from Turkey to Greek islands such as Lesbos, often in rubber boats. Thousands drowned in the Mediterranean that year. The photo of a drowned Kurdish boy, Alan Kurdi, on a Turkish beach shocked the world.

From Greece, columns of people walked up the Balkans toward Germany and Sweden. Hungary built a border fence. German Chancellor Angela Merkel kept Germany's borders open, saying "we can do this", and Germany took the largest share.

In 2016 the EU paid Turkey to stop the crossings, and numbers fell. The arrivals reshaped European politics and fuelled anti-immigrant parties. Compare the earlier, invited movement of Turkish workers to Germany.
sum: In 2015 more than a million people crossed into Europe to ask for asylum, the most in a single year since the Second World War. The largest group came from Syria, fleeing the civil war, with many also from Afghanistan and Iraq.
